original_question: For tilings of a finite simply-connected region in the hexagonal grid by stones and bones, there are two natural local 2-flip moves: one replaces two oppositely oriented stones by two bones, and the other replaces a stone-and-bone pair by a stone of the same orientation together with a bone of a different orientation. Can every such tiling be transformed into every other such tiling by a finite succession of these 2-flips?
target_in_paper: Section 9 (Miscellaneous), Problem 19: the 2-flip connectivity problem for stones-and-bones tilings of finite simply-connected regions in the hexagonal grid.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's intended problem very closely: it has the right ambient class of regions (finite simply-connected regions in the hexagonal grid), the correct tile family (stones and bones), the correct two local moves (the two natural 2-flips described immediately before Problem 19), and the correct global question of whether any two tilings can be connected by a finite sequence of those moves.
missing_details: The paper's ambient tile set is explicitly the five prototiles introduced earlier: two stones (right-pointing and left-pointing) and three bones (vertical, rising, and falling), together with all their translates.
To be fully stand-alone, the question should say that the two tilings being compared are tilings of the same finite simply-connected region.
The paper phrases the operation as 'mutated into ... by means of a succession of 2-flips'; your wording is equivalent, but the refined version should stay close to that official formulation.
The locality of the two moves is part of the setup: they are the specific local replacements shown in Figure 5, not arbitrary exchanges of two tiles.
The scope is all stones-and-bones tilings of such regions, not just benzels and not just the restricted type-112 case mentioned in the comment.

The nearby comment records two hidden assumptions/contextual facts that help delimit the exact problem: the simply-connected hypothesis is essential, and the restricted type-112 case is already known to be true.
refined_question: Let R be a finite simply-connected region of the hexagonal grid, and consider tilings of R by translates of the five stones-and-bones prototiles: the right stone, the left stone, and the vertical, rising, and falling bones. There are two natural local 2-flips: one replaces two stones of opposite orientation by two bones, and the other replaces a local stone-and-bone pair by a stone of the same orientation together with a bone of a different orientation. Must it be true that any stones-and-bones tiling of R can be mutated into any other stones-and-bones tiling of R by a finite succession of these 2-flips?
justification: This is essentially exactly Problem 19 of the paper. Section 1 supplies the intended meaning of 'stones and bones' by defining the five prototiles, and Section 9 introduces the two local 2-flips immediately before asking whether every tiling of a finite simply-connected region can be reached from every other by such moves. The only real sharpening needed is to make explicit that the two compared tilings are tilings of the same region and that the tile set consists of the five prototiles and their translates. The comment after Problem 19 shows that the simply-connectedness hypothesis is part of the exact problem and should not be removed, and that the already-solved type-112 case is only a special case, not the main target.
